newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - English castle owners lower drawbridge to public.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - English castle owners lower drawbridge to public.

text.p: Some things never change, not even after 700 years. The lord of Chillingham Castle is coming home for the weekend and the staff are in a frenzy.

The kitchen staff are preparing a banquet of venison and pheasant while gardener Alan Sanderson is busy stacking piles of wood to fuel the two cavernous fireplaces. The castle dogs snooze on window seats, dreaming of tasty morsels to come.

To be sure, the 50 guests for the "mediaeval banquet" are paying for the pleasure, and the castle owner, Sir Humphry Wakefield, makes no bones about why he invites visitors to share his private residence.
"You open enough to the public to make it from a white elephant into a grey elephant," he said in an interview at his castle near Alnwick in northeastern England.

Once a moated fortress, it still has crenellated towers, a fortified keep and a "dungeon" complete with Wakefield's collection of real torture devices ranging from racks to iron ladies -- spiked metal cages in human form that close on their victims.
The castle was the family seat of the aristocratic Grey family. Started in the 12th century, it was a genuine stronghold in the turbulent Borders region between Scotland and England.
As the border calmed down, it was gradually converted into a home. Windows were built into the grey stone walls, ceilings and walls were plastered and fancy fireplaces installed.
CASTLE RUIN GETS FACELIFT
But by 1932 when the 7th Earl of Tankerville, the Grey who then owned the castle, died, his son decided to pass on paying for the upkeep of a crumbling, and virtually unheatable, pile of stone.
Wakefield, whose wife Katherine is a Grey, bought the property in 1982. But 50 years of disuse had taken its toll. "Everything had gone, you know," he said. "Every damned ceiling had fallen in."

Wakefield, who has a private fortune and a professional interest in antiques, has filled the castle with artefacts from around the world. Paying visitors can poke around for a few hours or rent furnished apartments by the week.
Administrator Diane Phillips said 18,000 people visited the castle every year, with about 30 staying each week during the summer.
"You have to turn your hand to everything. You have to know you've got to clean the toilets or cook dinner," she said in between instructing cooks and directing the laying of the tables.
"GHOST TOURS" ON THE BATTLEMENTS
Even Wakefield has to help out. One member of staff has fallen ill so he must do a torchlit "ghost tour" himself.
"Come over here and look over the battlements," he commands the bemused guests he has led up onto the roof. "Don't be so wet (timid). If anyone falls over I'll have another ghost."
Wakefield revels in opening his castle to the public. "I love the public," he said. "It's like the applause at a lecture -- and they've all paid."

As he speaks, his staff set down before him platters of food, plates of cheese and a goblet of wine. Looking every inch the master of all he surveys, he dines alone at a wooden trestle table, fires blazing and faithful hound at his feet.

Many of Britain's noblest families have been forced by taxes, expensive upkeep -- replacing a roof can cost more than three million pounds ($5 million) -- and heating bills to open their family homes to a paying public.
Some, like Wakefield, keep virtually an open house. Others try to keep as much of a veneer of privacy as possible.
ARISTOCRATS SACRIFICE PRIVACY FOR CASH
Across the border in Scotland, Aline and Alexander Hay open their home, the 14th-century Duns Castle, to weddings, film crews and the occasional paying guest.
"My mother can't understand why I did it," Hay, who grew up in the castle, said.
The Hays dine with their visitors, making them feel as if they are guests. Others, like their neighbour, biscuit heir Lord Adrian Palmer, flee the paying tourists.
"The whole family's in that wing today," said a tour guide at Manderston, Palmer's 19th-century stately home that opens on Tuesday and Sunday afternoons.
"At 5.30 that rope comes down and they all pour out -- dogs and all."
Richard Wilkin, Director-General of Britain's Historic Houses Association, said it was not always easy for owners.
"There are obvious irritations," he said. "There is a wonderful moment of calm at five o' clock in the evening when the gates shut and you have it all to yourself."
LANDOWNERS FLEE TAXMAN
But owners knew they had an obligation to the public and were mostly happy to share their treaures.
"There's a very genuine feeling that it's something that, sure, they own it, but also they feel they are the guardians of it and it's not necessarily theirs exclusively," Wilkin said.
Many of the owners of castles and stately homes were escaping crippling inheritance taxes when they opened to one and all, Wilkin, whose organisation represents them, said.

"The arrangement has two aspects -- people who have been in receipt of public money in grants principally from English Heritage have to provide public access. They have to open for a certain number of days," he said.
Second, landowners can get a conditional exemption from inheritance tax for house, land or "important chattels" such as a collection of armour -- but in return have to provide public access to it.
Wilkin said the arrangements benefited everybody.
"These are really important entities -- it's not only the house but the works of art in the house and the garden," he said.

"If you are hit by inheritance tax every generation, that entity is dispersed and the public doesn't get to see it. Also if you are hit by inheritance tax, you can't repair the roof and then it isn't there either."
CASTLES PROVIDE TOURIST ATTRACTION
Owners were better at preserving the houses than organisations like the National Trust or English Heritage, he added.
And they were great for tourism. Wilkin said 11.5 million people visited historic homes in Britain each year.
"They are central to the tourist industry. They not only are they attractions but also they are the honeypots for all the other things like hotels."
But sometimes the price for maintaining public treasures is high.

Last year Palmer and Hay were turned out of the queen's Scottish honorary bodyguard, the Royal Company of Archers, for allowing their homes to be used in a film about Princess Diana's affair with cavalry officer James Hewitt.
